headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4%, its first increase since 2023, and warns inflation could near 5%

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings.
The Monetary Policy Committee, the nine-member Bank of England group that votes on interest rates.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4%, its first increase since 2023, and warns inflation could near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, from 3.75% to 4%, on 5 November 2026. It is the first increase since August 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1, and the one dissenter wanted a larger rise of 0.5 points, to 4.25%.
The Bank blamed energy prices linked to the war involving Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. It warned that inflation, which was 3.5% in September, could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said the move should not be read as the start of a long run of rises. He added that unless the Middle East conflict is resolved, it does not look like the last increase either. Markets saw roughly a one-in-four chance of another rise in December, and the next meeting is on 17 December. Earlier reports said two-year mortgage rates had already climbed by nearly half a point since early September.
levels.why: Borrowing costs, mortgages and savings rates all move with Bank Rate, and the Bank expects prices to keep climbing.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts interest rates to 4% and sees inflation heading towards 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate, Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. The decision on 5 November was the first rise since August 2023. Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed a quarter-point increase, while one wanted a bigger half-point rise.
The Bank pointed to higher energy prices caused by the Middle East conflict. It now expects inflation, 3.5% in September, to reach around 5% by mid-2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the first of many. But he said that if the conflict is not resolved, this is unlikely to be the final increase. Traders thought there was about a one-in-four chance of another rise at the next meeting on 17 December. Benchmark two-year mortgage rates had already risen by nearly half a percentage point since the start of September.
levels.why: Households with mortgages or loans may face higher costs, and savers may see better rates.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates for the first time in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its key interest rate from 3.75% to 4%, the first increase since August 2023. The committee that sets the rate voted 8 to 1 for a quarter-point rise. One member wanted a half-point rise instead.
Officials said energy prices, pushed up by the conflict in the Middle East, are driving inflation. They expect the rate of price rises to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027, up from 3.5% in September.
Bank Governor Andrew Bailey said people should not take this as the start of a long series of increases. However, he said that unless the conflict ends, it does not look like the last rise. Financial markets see about a one-in-four chance of another increase in December. Mortgage rates had already been rising for weeks before the decision.
levels.why: Higher rates make borrowing dearer, which affects homeowners, renters and businesses.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4% as energy costs push prices higher
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years. The main rate went up from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November, after eight of the nine decision-makers voted for the quarter-point rise. The ninth wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank says high energy prices, linked to the war in the Middle East, are pushing up the cost of living. It thinks prices could be rising at about 5% a year by the middle of next year. In September the figure was 3.5%.
Governor Andrew Bailey said this is not necessarily the first step in a long run of rises. But he said more rises look likely if the conflict carries on. The next decision is due on 17 December, and markets think there is a one-in-four chance of another increase then.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has raised interest rates, and says prices could rise faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%. This is the rate that influences what banks charge for loans and mortgages, and what they pay savers. It is the first rise since 2023. Eight of nine experts on the Bank's committee voted for it. One wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank did this because prices are going up faster, mostly because energy costs more after the conflict in the Middle East. Prices rose 3.5% over the year to September. The Bank thinks they could be rising by about 5% a year by the middle of 2027.
The Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey, said this is not the start of lots of rises. But he said there could be more if the conflict goes on. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Mortgages and loans could cost more, though savers might earn a little more.

levels.headline: Interest rates in the UK go up to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates. The main rate is now 4%. Before, it was 3.75%. It is the first rise in over three years. The Bank is the part of the country that looks after how much borrowing costs.
Why did it do this? Prices are going up faster. Energy costs more because of fighting in the Middle East. When prices rise like this, it is called inflation. Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September. The Bank thinks they could rise by about 5% a year by the middle of next year.
A higher rate makes loans and mortgages cost more. That can make people spend less, which helps slow price rises. Savers may get paid a little more. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could come if the fighting goes on.
levels.why: Families with loans or mortgages may have to pay more each month.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to try to slow rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates. They went from 3.75% to 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or the extra you get when you save. The Bank sets the main rate, and banks follow it.
Prices are rising faster than the Bank wants. This is called inflation. Fuel and energy cost more because of a war in the Middle East. Prices went up 3.5% in the year to September, and the Bank thinks they may reach about 5% next year.
By making borrowing cost more, the Bank hopes people spend less. Then prices should rise more slowly. But it also means people with a mortgage may pay more each month. The Bank's boss said there may be more rises if the war carries on.
levels.why: Your family's loans could cost more, but the Bank hopes prices will stop rising so fast.

levels.headline: The Bank of England puts up interest rates to slow price rises
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, and the extra you earn when you save. The Bank sets the main rate, and banks and building societies follow it.
Why now? Prices are rising faster. We call that inflation. Energy costs more because of fighting in the Middle East, and that makes many other things dearer. Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, and the Bank thinks they could rise by about 5% a year by next summer.
The Bank hopes that dearer borrowing makes people spend a bit less, so prices rise more slowly. The downside is that mortgages and loans can cost more each month. The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could come if the fighting carries on.
levels.why: Your family's loans and savings can change when this rate changes.

levels.headline: Interest rates have gone up in Britain
levels.body:
The Bank of England is in charge of interest rates. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow money. It went up today from 3.75 to 4 out of every 100 pounds. That is a small step up.
Why did it go up? Things in shops cost more than before, and petrol and gas cost more too. This is because of fighting in another part of the world. Grown-ups call this inflation. It means your money buys less than it did.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less. Then prices might stop rising so fast. But families who borrowed money to buy a home may have to pay a bit extra every month. The people at the Bank say prices might keep rising for a while, and rates could go up again.
levels.why: It changes how much families pay back on loans, and the Bank hopes it keeps prices steady.

levels.headline: The bank that looks after Britain's money made borrowing cost a bit more
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow a toy from a friend and promise to give back a little extra as a thank you. That extra is called interest. In Britain, one big bank decides how much extra is normal. It is called the Bank of England.
This week the bank said the extra should be a bit bigger. It went from 3.75 to 4 coins in every 100.
Why? Lots of things in shops now cost more, like food and fuel. The bank wants prices to stop going up so fast. When borrowing costs more, people buy fewer things. Then shops do not need to raise prices as much. It is a bit like when everyone wants the last biscuit, so it costs more. If fewer people want it, the price stays small. Some grown-ups will have to pay a bit more.
levels.why: It is one way the grown-ups try to stop everything getting more expensive.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 4.36% as AI-led sell-off pushes the Nasdaq into correction

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 of the largest companies listed in the United States.
A fall of more than 10% from a recent peak in an index or share price.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 4.36% as AI-led sell-off pushes the Nasdaq into correction
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Thursday 5 November, the last completed US session, falling 4.36% to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to 51,523.06. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% to 24,315.00.
The Nasdaq ended more than 10% below the record it set last month, which is known as a correction. The small-company Russell 2000 index also entered a correction after falling 4.45%. All 11 sectors of the S&P 500 finished lower, and technology fell 7.30%.
CNBC linked the fall to fears that Democratic wins in the midterm elections could slow the building of AI data centres. Nvidia and Qualcomm each fell more than 9%, and Qualcomm also gave a disappointing forecast for the current quarter. The sell-off wiped out the Dow's 1,569-point jump on the previous day.
levels.why: Falls this size hit pension funds and savings, and show how nervous investors are about AI company valuations.

levels.headline: US stocks slump as S&P 500 drops 4.36% and Nasdaq enters correction
levels.body:
US shares fell sharply on Thursday 5 November, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 closed down 4.36% at 7,353.73, the Dow lost 3.44% (1,833.06 points) to finish at 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00.
The Nasdaq is now more than 10% below its record from last month, which traders call a correction. Smaller companies suffered too, with the Russell 2000 down 4.45%. Every sector of the S&P 500 fell, and technology was worst, down 7.30%.
Investors were worried that Democratic election gains could slow spending on AI data centres. Chip makers led the drop, with Nvidia and Qualcomm both down more than 9%. Qualcomm also warned of weaker results ahead. The losses cancelled the large Dow gain from the day before.
levels.why: Many pension funds and savings accounts hold US shares, so big falls can affect ordinary savers.

levels.headline: Wall Street sinks as tech shares tumble: S&P 500 down 4.36%
levels.body:
Wall Street suffered a steep sell-off on Thursday 5 November, the most recent full trading day. The S&P 500 ended down 4.36% at 7,353.73. The Dow Jones fell 1,833 points, or 3.44%, to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq dropped 5.52% to 24,315.00.
The Nasdaq has now fallen more than 10% from its record high of last month, a move known as a correction. Technology shares were hit hardest, falling 7.30% as a group, and all other sectors of the S&P 500 also closed lower.
CNBC reported that investors feared Democratic wins in the midterms could slow the building of data centres for artificial intelligence. Nvidia and Qualcomm each lost more than 9% of their value, and Qualcomm gave a weak outlook. Much of the previous day's rally was wiped out.
levels.why: The fall shows how much of the market now depends on AI companies.

levels.headline: US stock market has its worst day in months, with the S&P 500 down 4.36%
levels.body:
The US stock market had a bad day on Thursday 5 November. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 of America's biggest companies, closed down 4.36% at 7,353.73. The Dow, another well-known measure, fell 3.44% to 51,523.06. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, fell 5.52% to 24,315.00.
The Nasdaq is now more than 10% below its record from last month. Traders call that a correction. Every part of the S&P 500 fell, with technology down the most.
Investors are worried that political changes after the midterm elections could slow the building of data centres that power artificial intelligence. Shares in chip makers Nvidia and Qualcomm each dropped more than 9%. The falls undid the previous day's big gains.
levels.why: If shares stay low, people's pensions and savings could be worth less.

levels.headline: American shares fall sharply, led by technology companies
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States fell a lot on Thursday 5 November. A share is a small part of a company that you can buy. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big American companies, fell by 4.36%. It ended the day at 7,353.73. Another list, the Dow, fell 3.44%. The Nasdaq, full of tech companies, fell 5.52%.
The Nasdaq is now more than 10% lower than its best level last month. People who follow the markets call this a correction.
Why did it happen? Some investors worry that new political leaders in America might slow down the building of big computer centres used for artificial intelligence. Two chip firms, Nvidia and Qualcomm, each lost more than 9% of their value. One of them also said its next results may be weak.
levels.why: Many people's pensions are invested in shares, so big falls can matter to them.

levels.headline: Share prices in America dropped a lot on Thursday
levels.body:
Share prices in America dropped on Thursday. A share is a tiny piece of a company. When many people sell their shares, prices fall. That happened on Thursday 5 November.
There are lists that follow the biggest companies. The S&P 500 list went down by about 4 out of every 100. The Dow list went down by about 3.4 out of 100. The Nasdaq list, which has lots of technology firms, went down by more than 5 out of 100. That is a big drop for one day.
Why? Some investors are worried about big computer centres for artificial intelligence, called AI. They think new election results might slow down the building of these centres. Two chip makers, Nvidia and Qualcomm, lost more than 9% of their value. Pension savings can go down when shares fall.
levels.why: Money saved for retirement is often invested in shares, so a drop can matter.

levels.headline: American company shares fell by a lot
levels.body:
On Thursday, the price of shares in American companies fell a lot. A share is a small piece of a company. If you own one, you own a tiny part of that company. When lots of people want to sell, the price goes down.
The main list of 500 big companies fell by more than four in every hundred. The tech list fell by more than five in every hundred. It is as if a toy that cost 100 pounds suddenly cost 96.
Why did this happen? People who own shares got worried about companies that make computer brains, called AI. They are not sure if these companies will keep growing so fast. Two chip makers lost almost a tenth of their value in one day. Sometimes prices go back up, and sometimes they stay low.
levels.why: Many families save for the future by owning shares, so falls can worry them.

levels.headline: Share prices in America fall as worries about technology grow
levels.body:
Share prices in America fell sharply on Thursday 5 November. A share is a small part of a company that you can buy. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big American companies, fell by 4.36%. The Dow list fell by 3.44%, and the Nasdaq list fell by 5.52%.
The Nasdaq is now more than 10% below its highest level, set last month. Traders call that a correction. Every part of the S&P 500 fell, and technology fell the most.
Investors are worried that new political leaders might slow down the building of big computer centres for artificial intelligence. Two chip makers, Nvidia and Qualcomm, each lost more than 9% of their value. Many pensions hold shares, so a fall like this can matter to ordinary families.
levels.why: Pensions and savings are often invested in shares, so falls can matter.

levels.headline: Share prices in America dropped by a lot in one day
levels.body:
On Thursday, the price of shares in American companies dropped a lot. A share is a tiny piece of a company. If many people want to sell, the price goes down.
The main list of 500 big companies went down by about four in every hundred. The list with lots of technology firms went down by more than five in every hundred. That is a big fall for just one day.
Some people are worried about the big computer centres that run artificial intelligence, called AI. They think the building of them might slow down. Two chip firms, Nvidia and Qualcomm, lost almost a tenth of their value. Prices can go back up, but nobody knows when. Grown-ups who save for the future may feel worried.
levels.why: Savings for the future are often tied to share prices.

levels.headline: Prices of company shares went down a lot
levels.body:
Do you remember swapping stickers in the playground? A sticker is worth more when everyone wants it. A share in a company works a bit like that. Lots of grown-ups buy and sell them.
On Thursday, many grown-ups in America wanted to sell their shares all at once. So the prices went down. The main score for 500 big companies dropped by about four in every hundred. Think of it like a sweet jar losing a few sweets.
Most of the sellers owned shares in companies that make clever computers. They were worried that these companies might not grow as fast as hoped. Two of the companies lost almost one tenth of their value in a single day. Prices can go up again, but it can take time. Some people felt worried, and others stayed calm.
levels.why: It shows even grown-ups can feel worried about money.

headline: Tech sell-off wipes $1 trillion from the Magnificent 7 and spreads to Asian chip makers

terms.meaning: A nickname for seven giant US technology companies whose shares have a big influence on the stock market.
The total worth of a company's shares, found by multiplying the share price by the number of shares.

levels.headline: Tech sell-off wipes $1 trillion from the Magnificent 7 and spreads to Asian chip makers
levels.body:
The sell-off in technology shares on Thursday 5 November wiped about $1 trillion from the combined value of the so-called Magnificent 7 giants, CNBC reported. Nvidia lost almost $450 billion in market value, and it and Qualcomm each fell more than 9%. The Nasdaq had its worst day since April 2025.
Qualcomm's weak forecast for the current quarter added to worries that spending on artificial intelligence data centres may slow. Top Democrats have called for limits on the AI building boom after the midterm elections, and one called for a national data centre moratorium.
The fall spread to Asia on Friday 6 November. SK Hynix fell more than 8% and Samsung Electronics lost about 7%. CNBC also reported that Japan's Nikkei 225 entered a bear market, and that Softbank and TSMC were among the shares to tumble.
levels.why: Chip makers sit at the heart of the AI boom, so their falls can spread across global markets.

levels.headline: A $1 trillion loss for big tech as the AI sell-off reaches Asia
levels.body:
The technology sell-off on Thursday 5 November cut about $1 trillion from the combined value of the Magnificent 7, the group of giant US tech firms. Nvidia alone lost almost $450 billion, and both Nvidia and Qualcomm dropped more than 9%. The Nasdaq had its worst day since April 2025.
Qualcomm gave a disappointing outlook, and investors fear less spending on AI data centres. After the midterms, senior Democrats called for tougher controls on the AI building boom, with one demanding a national moratorium on data centres.
On Friday 6 November the losses reached Asia. SK Hynix fell more than 8% and Samsung Electronics about 7%. Softbank and TSMC also dropped, and CNBC reported that Japan's Nikkei 225 had entered a bear market.
levels.why: A slowdown in AI spending would affect firms, jobs and markets around the world.

levels.headline: Big tech loses $1 trillion in a day as the sell-off spreads to Asia
levels.body:
Shares in the big American technology companies known as the Magnificent 7 lost about $1 trillion in value on Thursday 5 November. Chip maker Nvidia alone lost nearly $450 billion, and Nvidia and Qualcomm each fell more than 9%. The Nasdaq had its worst day since April 2025.
Investors are concerned that spending on artificial intelligence data centres could slow down. Qualcomm gave a weak forecast, and leading Democrats have called for limits on data centre building after their election wins.
The fall spread to Asia on Friday. South Korea's SK Hynix lost more than 8% and Samsung Electronics about 7%. Softbank and TSMC also fell, and Japan's Nikkei 225 index moved into a bear market, which means a fall of 20% or more from its high.
levels.why: The AI boom has driven many markets, so a wobble in it is felt worldwide.

levels.headline: Tech shares slide worldwide as US giants lose $1 trillion
levels.body:
Some of the world's biggest technology companies lost a huge amount of value on Thursday 5 November. The group nicknamed the Magnificent 7 lost about $1 trillion in total. Chip maker Nvidia lost nearly $450 billion, and its shares fell more than 9%, as did Qualcomm's.
The cause was worry about whether spending on the data centres that run artificial intelligence will keep growing. Qualcomm gave a weak outlook, and some leading Democrats want to limit data centre building after the midterms.
The fall then reached Asia on Friday 6 November. SK Hynix dropped more than 8%, and Samsung lost about 7%. Softbank and TSMC also fell. Japan's main share index, the Nikkei 225, entered what traders call a bear market, meaning a fall of 20% or more.
levels.why: If AI spending slows, it could affect jobs and share prices in many countries.

levels.headline: Big tech firms lose $1 trillion as share falls spread to Asia
levels.body:
Big technology firms lost a huge amount of value on Thursday 5 November. Seven giant American companies, nicknamed the Magnificent 7, lost about $1 trillion between them. That is a very large sum. One chip firm, Nvidia, lost nearly $450 billion on its own. Its shares and those of Qualcomm each fell more than 9%.
Investors are worried that companies may spend less on the computer centres needed for artificial intelligence. After the election, some Democrats said there should be limits on building them.
On Friday the falls reached Asia. Shares in the Korean firms SK Hynix and Samsung dropped more than 8% and about 7%. Japan's main share index also entered a bear market, which means it has fallen by 20% or more.
levels.why: Many people around the world have savings linked to these firms.

levels.headline: Technology company shares fall in America and then in Asia
levels.body:
On Thursday, shares in big technology companies fell a lot in America. Seven very large firms lost about $1 trillion in value together. That is a huge amount of money. One chip company, Nvidia, lost nearly $450 billion of it.
Chips are tiny parts inside computers and phones. They are also needed for artificial intelligence, or AI. Some investors now worry that firms will spend less on AI computer centres. One chip firm also said its next results might be weak.
On Friday, the falls spread to Asia. Shares in the Korean firms SK Hynix and Samsung fell by about 8% and 7%. In Japan, the main share index fell so far that it is now in what experts call a bear market. That means a drop of one fifth or more.
levels.why: Shares in tech firms are held in many pensions, so the falls can matter.

levels.headline: Tech firms lose a huge amount of money value in one day
levels.body:
Some of the biggest tech companies in the world became worth much less on Thursday. Together, seven American firms lost about $1 trillion. Each has a value, which is the price of all its shares added together. One chip firm lost almost $450 billion.
Chips are tiny parts that make computers work. They are needed for AI, which is computer software that can do smart jobs. People are worried that firms may not spend as much on AI in future, so they sold their shares.
On Friday, the same thing happened in Asia. Two big Korean firms lost about 8% and 7% of their value. In Japan, a main list of shares fell by one fifth or more from its top. Experts call that a bear market. Prices might recover, but nobody knows when.
levels.why: It shows that things based on big hopes for AI can swing a lot.

levels.headline: Big technology firms lose a huge amount of value
levels.body:
Some of the biggest technology companies in the world lost a lot of value on Thursday. Seven American firms, nicknamed the Magnificent 7, lost about $1 trillion together. That is a giant number. One chip firm, Nvidia, lost nearly $450 billion by itself.
Chips are tiny parts inside computers. They are needed for artificial intelligence, or AI. Investors worry that firms may spend less on AI computer centres, so they sold their shares.
On Friday the same thing happened in Asia. Two big Korean firms, SK Hynix and Samsung, lost about 8% and 7%. In Japan, the main share list fell into what experts call a bear market, a drop of one fifth or more. Prices could recover, but nobody can be sure.
levels.why: It shows how much the world's markets now depend on AI hopes.

levels.headline: Some very big computer companies became worth much less
levels.body:
Some of the biggest companies in the world make things for computers. On Thursday, many people sold their shares in them, so they became worth less. Seven big firms lost about a trillion dollars. That is more than anyone can count on fingers and toes.
Why did they sell? The firms make tiny parts for clever computers called AI. People started to worry that the firms might not sell as many parts as they hoped. It is a bit like a sweet shop that thought everyone would buy lots of sweets, then found fewer children came.
On Friday, the same worry reached Asia, where other firms that make computer parts also lost value. This does not mean they will stay low. Prices go up and down all the time.
levels.why: It reminds us that prices can drop when people are unsure about the future.

levels.headline: A playground worry about computer companies
levels.body:
Imagine everyone in the playground is excited about a new game. Lots of children trade stickers to get a part in it. The stickers become very valuable. Then one day some children say, maybe the game is not so good after all. Suddenly many of them want to sell their stickers at the same time.
That is a bit like what happened on Thursday. The stickers are shares in big computer companies. The new game is clever computer software called AI. Some grown-ups got worried the game might not grow as fast as hoped, so they sold. Seven companies lost a huge amount of value.
On Friday, children in other places, in Asia, got worried too, and their sticker prices fell. Prices can go up again, and often do.
levels.why: It is a reminder that excitement and worry can both change what things are worth.

headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for the first time in three years, with an ECB rate rise looming

terms.meaning: The group of European Union countries that use the euro as their currency.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the euro zone.

levels.headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for the first time in three years, with an ECB rate rise looming
levels.body:
Euro zone inflation rose to 4% in the 12 months to October, up from 3.8% in September, according to the flash estimate published on 4 November. It is the highest reading since September 2023, when it was 4.3%.
Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier, adding roughly 1.9 percentage points to the headline figure. Reporting linked this to the Iran war. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.5%. Italy's rate jumped to 5.6% from 4.2%, while Germany's fell to 2.8%, mainly because of a fuel tax cut from 1 October.
The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after raising it in June and September. Markets see about an 84% chance of a quarter-point rise at its meeting on 16 and 17 December.
levels.why: Higher inflation squeezes households and raises the chance of costlier borrowing across Europe.

levels.headline: Euro zone inflation reaches 4%, highest in three years
levels.body:
Inflation across the euro zone rose to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, a first estimate showed on 4 November. That is the highest since September 2023.
The main cause was energy, which cost 20.8% more than a year before and added about 1.9 percentage points to the total. Reports tied this to the war involving Iran. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, stayed at 2.5%. Italy saw the biggest rise, from 4.2% to 5.6%, whereas Germany's rate fell to 2.8% helped by a cut in fuel tax.
The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October after rises in June and September. Traders think there is about an 84% chance it will raise rates by a quarter point at the 16 and 17 December meeting.
levels.why: It could mean dearer loans for families and firms across Europe.

levels.headline: Prices rise faster in the euro zone: inflation hits 4%
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro rose 4% in the year to October, faster than the 3.8% in September. A first estimate on 4 November showed it was the highest figure in three years.
Energy was the main reason. Energy costs were 20.8% higher than a year ago, linked in reports to the Iran war. Prices excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco rose 2.5%, the same as before. Italy's inflation jumped to 5.6%, while Germany's dropped to 2.8% after a cut in fuel tax.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the euro zone, held its rate at 2.5% on 29 October. Financial markets now think it is about 84% likely to raise rates by a quarter point in December.
levels.why: Higher prices and borrowing costs would be felt by households across the euro area.

levels.headline: Inflation in the euro zone climbs to 4%, a three-year high
levels.body:
Prices across the euro zone are rising faster. Inflation reached 4% in the year to October, compared with 3.8% in September. It is the highest in three years, according to a first estimate published on 4 November.
The biggest factor was the cost of energy, which was 20.8% higher than a year earlier. Reports connected that with the war involving Iran. Excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose 2.5%. Italy's rate jumped to 5.6%, but Germany's fell to 2.8% because the government cut fuel tax.
The European Central Bank kept its main rate at 2.5% on 29 October. Traders think there is an 84% chance it will raise the rate by a quarter of a point in December, to help slow price rises.
levels.why: People in Europe may find shopping and borrowing costs rising.

levels.headline: Prices in countries using the euro are rising faster
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that share the euro are going up faster. This is called inflation. In the year to October, prices rose by 4%. In September it was 3.8%. This is the highest it has been for three years.
The main reason is energy. It cost more than a fifth more than a year ago. Reports link this to the war involving Iran. If you leave out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose 2.5%. In Italy prices rose 5.6%, but in Germany only 2.8%, partly because Germany cut a fuel tax.
The European Central Bank looks after interest rates for these countries. It left the rate at 2.5% last month, but traders think it may raise it in December.
levels.why: It means everyday things cost more, and loans could cost more too.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster in Europe
levels.body:
In many European countries, people pay in euros. Prices there are going up faster. This is called inflation. In the year to October, prices rose by 4%. It was 3.8% the month before. This is the highest in three years.
The main reason is that energy costs a lot more. It was about a fifth dearer than a year ago. People link this to a war in the Middle East. In Italy, prices rose 5.6%. In Germany they rose 2.8%, because the country cut a tax on fuel.
The European Central Bank sets the main interest rate for these countries. It kept the rate at 2.5% last month. But traders think it may raise it in December to slow prices down.
levels.why: Families may pay more for food, fuel and loans.

levels.headline: Shop prices go up faster across Europe
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe share the same money, the euro. Prices in those countries are going up faster now. When prices rise, we call it inflation. Over the last year, prices went up by 4 out of every 100. A month before, it was 3.8. This is the highest it has been in three years.
A big reason is energy, like fuel for cars and gas for heating. It costs about a fifth more than last year. People link this to fighting in the Middle East. In Italy, prices went up by 5.6. In Germany, it was 2.8, because Germany cut a fuel tax.
The bank that looks after the euro may raise its interest rate in December. That would make borrowing cost more.
levels.why: Families in Europe may have less money left after paying bills.

levels.headline: Prices in euro countries rise faster than they have for three years
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro are rising faster. We call this inflation. In the year to October, prices went up by 4%. A month earlier it was 3.8%. It is the highest figure for three years.
The main reason is energy, such as fuel and gas. It costs about a fifth more than a year ago, and reports link this to the war involving Iran. In Italy prices rose 5.6%. In Germany they rose only 2.8%, partly because Germany cut a fuel tax.
The European Central Bank sets the main interest rate for these countries. It left the rate at 2.5% last month, but traders think it may raise it in December to slow price rises. That would make borrowing dearer.
levels.why: Families in Europe could pay more for shopping and for loans.

levels.headline: Things cost more in Europe than a year ago
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the same money, called the euro. In these countries, things are costing more than they did a year ago. On average, prices are up by 4 pounds in every 100 pounds. That is the biggest rise for three years.
Why is this happening? Energy, like fuel and gas, costs about a fifth more than before. People say this is because of a war far away. In Italy prices rose even more, by 5.6 in every 100. In Germany it was 2.8, since Germany took some tax off fuel.
A bank in charge of the euro could now make borrowing cost more. It does this to slow price rises. It will decide in December.
levels.why: Your family's money can buy less when prices go up.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe go up faster, like sweets getting more expensive
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweet cost 100 pence last year. This year it costs 104 pence. That is what 4% means. It may not sound like a lot. But when lots of things cost more, pocket money does not stretch as far.
This is happening in countries in Europe that share the euro. The biggest reason is the cost of energy, like fuel and gas. It costs about a fifth more than last year. This is because of fighting in the Middle East. In Italy, things cost 5.6% more. In Germany, only 2.8% more.
A big bank may make borrowing cost more in December. Then people buy less, and prices may stop rising so fast.
levels.why: It means pocket money, and grown-ups' pay, buys a little less.

headline: Supreme Court hears two-day appeal against the Palestine Action ban as police arrest supporters outside

terms.meaning: A government ban that makes membership of, or support for, a group a crime.
The highest court in the UK for most cases.

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears two-day appeal against the Palestine Action ban as police arrest supporters outside
levels.body:
The UK Supreme Court heard a two-day appeal on Wednesday 4 and Thursday 5 November against the government's ban on Palestine Action. No judgment has been given, and Euronews found no date for one.
The challenge is brought by co-founder Huda Ammori, who was granted permission to appeal on a narrow procedural ground: that the Home Office did not follow its own criteria. The High Court ruled in Ammori's favour in February, but the Court of Appeal later found the ban was not unlawful. She has said she would go to the European Court of Human Rights if she loses.
Police said 25 people were detained outside the court on 4 November on suspicion of supporting a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act, with more arrests expected. Supporting the group is a criminal offence, and the outcome could affect charges brought under the ban.
levels.why: The case tests how far the state can go in banning a protest group as terrorist.

levels.headline: Palestine Action ban reaches the Supreme Court, with arrests outside
levels.body:
The Supreme Court in London heard the appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action on Wednesday 4 and Thursday 5 November. Judges have not yet ruled, and no date for a ruling has been reported.
Co-founder Huda Ammori brings the case on a narrow procedural ground, arguing that the Home Office failed to follow its own criteria. The High Court agreed with her in February, but the government appealed and the Court of Appeal decided the ban was not unlawful. Ammori says she would take the case to the European Court of Human Rights if necessary.
Police detained 25 people outside the court on 4 November on suspicion of supporting a banned group under the Terrorism Act, and said more arrests were likely. The result could affect people already charged.
levels.why: It could decide whether people can still be prosecuted for supporting the group.

levels.headline: Supreme Court hears challenge to Palestine Action ban
levels.body:
The UK's Supreme Court has spent two days, 4 and 5 November, hearing an appeal against the ban on the protest group Palestine Action. The judges have not yet announced a decision.
The appeal is led by the group's co-founder, Huda Ammori. She argues on a narrow point: that the Home Office did not follow its own rules when it decided to ban the group. The High Court agreed with her in February, but the Court of Appeal later said the ban was lawful. If she loses, she has said she will go to the European Court of Human Rights.
Outside the court, police arrested supporters. They said 25 people were detained on 4 November on suspicion of backing a banned group, and more arrests were expected. Supporting the group is a crime under the Terrorism Act.
levels.why: It matters for protest rights and for people facing charges over the ban.

levels.headline: UK's highest court hears appeal over the Palestine Action ban
levels.body:
The UK's highest court, the Supreme Court, has heard an appeal against the government's ban on Palestine Action. The hearing ran for two days, on 4 and 5 November, and the judges have not yet decided.
The case is brought by the group's co-founder, Huda Ammori. She says the Home Office did not follow its own criteria when it banned the group, which counts as a terrorist organisation in law. A lower court agreed with her in February. But the Court of Appeal disagreed, so the ban stayed. She says she would take the case to a European court if she loses.
Police detained 25 people outside the court on 4 November on suspicion of supporting a banned group, and more arrests were expected. Backing a banned group is a crime.
levels.why: The decision could change how the government is able to ban groups.

levels.headline: The Supreme Court has heard an appeal about banning Palestine Action
levels.body:
The Supreme Court is the top court in the UK. This week it heard a case about a ban on a group called Palestine Action. The hearing lasted two days, 4 and 5 November. The judges have not said yet what they have decided.
The government banned the group by calling it a terrorist group. This is called proscription. It means that being a member or supporting the group is a crime. Huda Ammori, who helped start the group, says the government did not follow its own rules when it made the ban. One court agreed with her in February, but a higher one did not.
Police arrested supporters outside the court. They said 25 people were held on 4 November, and they expected more arrests.
levels.why: It shows how courts check what the government is allowed to ban.

levels.headline: Top UK court hears case on a banned protest group
levels.body:
The top court in the UK, the Supreme Court, held a hearing on 4 and 5 November. It was about a group called Palestine Action. The government has banned the group by saying it is a terrorist group. Under the ban, it is a crime to be a member or to show support.
One of the group's founders, Huda Ammori, says the ban was not done properly. She says the Home Office did not follow its own rules. A court agreed with her in February. Then a higher court said the ban was fine. So she went to the Supreme Court.
The judges have not yet said what they have decided. Outside the court, police arrested supporters. They said 25 people were held on 4 November, and more arrests were expected.
levels.why: Courts make sure that governments follow their own rules.

levels.headline: Judges hear a case about a banned group
levels.body:
This week, the most senior judges in the UK heard a case. It was about a group called Palestine Action. The government banned the group. It said the group was terrorist. After the ban, it became a crime to be part of the group or to say you back it.
A woman called Huda Ammori helped start the group. She says the government made a mistake in how it made the ban. She says it did not follow its own rules. Some judges agreed with her, and some did not. So the top court, the Supreme Court, had to listen on 4 and 5 November.
The judges have not decided yet. Outside, police arrested 25 people on 4 November for showing support.
levels.why: It decides whether the government followed fair rules when it banned a group.

levels.headline: The UK's top court hears a case about a banned group
levels.body:
The Supreme Court is the highest court in the UK. On 4 and 5 November it heard a case about a group called Palestine Action. The government banned the group by calling it a terrorist group. That means being a member, or showing support, is a crime.
One of the group's founders, Huda Ammori, says the ban was not done properly because the Home Office did not follow its own rules. One court agreed with her in February. A higher court did not, so she took the case to the Supreme Court.
The judges have not yet said what they have decided. Outside, police arrested 25 people on 4 November on suspicion of supporting a banned group, and said they expected more arrests.
levels.why: It tests whether the government followed fair rules when it banned a group.

levels.headline: Britain's top judges listen to a case about a banned group
levels.body:
The most important judges in Britain have been listening to a case. It is about a group named Palestine Action. The government banned it because it said the group was too dangerous. When a group is banned, people can get in trouble for joining it or saying they support it.
One of the people who started the group says the ban is not fair. She says the government did not follow its own steps. Judges have not decided yet. They listened for two days, 4 and 5 November.
Outside the building, police arrested 25 people on 4 November. They had signs or messages saying they backed the group. Nobody knows yet what the judges will say.
levels.why: It shows that even the government has to follow rules.

levels.headline: Grown-up judges listen to an argument about a ban
levels.body:
Imagine a school has a rule saying a club is not allowed. Some children in the club say, the teachers did not follow the right steps to ban us. That is a bit like this story, but it is about the whole country.
The government banned a group called Palestine Action. After the ban, it became a crime to join it. One of the people who started the group says the ban was not done by the rules. So the top judges in the country listened to both sides on 4 and 5 November.
They have not said who is right yet. Outside the court, the police arrested 25 people. Judges will take time to think before they decide.
levels.why: It is about making sure everyone, even leaders, follows the rules.

headline: Ukraine, Russia and the US plan Abu Dhabi talks on 10 and 11 November as Russian strikes continue

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, either for a short time or permanently.
An exchange of captured soldiers between two sides in a war.

levels.headline: Ukraine, Russia and the US plan Abu Dhabi talks on 10 and 11 November as Russian strikes continue
levels.body:
Ukraine, Russia and the United States will hold talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, mediated by US officials. US envoy Steve Witkoff announced the meeting, and Zelenskyy, the Kremlin and Washington have all confirmed it. It would be the first three-way talks since February. The agenda is said to cover security arrangements and de-escalation.
Russia's delegation is expected to be led by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
Strikes are clouding the outlook. Zelenskyy said Russia launched 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles overnight on 3 November, and he said more than 50 people were trapped under rubble after a strike on a school used as an aid centre. A short truce ended at the weekend. Earlier Abu Dhabi rounds in January and February produced a 314-prisoner swap but no deal on Donbas.
levels.why: The talks are the best current chance of reducing fighting, but heavy strikes make progress hard.

levels.headline: US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks set for Abu Dhabi as attacks go on
levels.body:
A new round of talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, is planned for 10 and 11 November in Abu Dhabi. US envoy Steve Witkoff announced it, and Kyiv, Moscow and Washington have confirmed it. These would be the first talks involving all three since February, and are said to focus on security arrangements and de-escalation.
Moscow's team is to be led by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky. Meanwhile the fighting continues. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles overnight on 3 November. More than 50 people were reported trapped under rubble after a strike on a school-turned-aid centre.
A brief truce ended at the weekend. In earlier talks in January and February, the sides agreed a swap of 314 prisoners but not a settlement on the Donbas region.
levels.why: Any deal could affect European security, energy prices and the future of the war.

levels.headline: Fresh Ukraine peace talks planned in Abu Dhabi despite heavy Russian strikes
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November for talks mediated by the United States. US envoy Steve Witkoff announced the date. Ukraine, Russia and the US have all confirmed it. It will be the first meeting of the three sides since February, and it is expected to focus on security and on reducing the fighting.
Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to President Putin.
But the attacks have not stopped. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russia sent 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles in one night. He also said more than 50 people were trapped under a building hit in a strike on a school used as an aid centre. A short truce ended over the weekend. Earlier rounds led to a swap of 314 prisoners.
levels.why: Peace talks affect the safety of millions and the cost of energy across Europe.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia to meet for US-led peace talks in Abu Dhabi
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia will send teams to Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November for talks led by the United States. The date was announced by US envoy Steve Witkoff, and all three sides have agreed to it. It is the first such meeting since February. The talks are meant to look at security arrangements and ways to cool the conflict.
President Putin's aide, Vladimir Medinsky, will lead Russia's team.
The war goes on in the meantime. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russia attacked in one night with 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles. He also said that over 50 people were stuck under rubble after a strike on a school that was being used to give out aid. A short ceasefire ended at the weekend.
levels.why: Success or failure at the talks could shape the war and Europe's security.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia are going to talk again, even as attacks continue
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia are going to meet in Abu Dhabi, a city in the United Arab Emirates, on 10 and 11 November. The United States will help to run the talks. It is the first time all three have met since February. They plan to talk about security and how to calm things down.
There is little sign the fighting has eased. Ukraine's president said Russia sent 289 drones and 17 big missiles in a single night. He also said more than 50 people were trapped under rubble after a strike on a school that was being used to hand out aid. A short pause in the fighting ended at the weekend.
At talks earlier this year, the two sides swapped 314 prisoners but did not agree on who should control the Donbas region.
levels.why: Talks are the main way the war could end, so what happens matters to many people.

levels.headline: Peace talks on the war in Ukraine are planned for next week
levels.body:
Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the United States will meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. They want to talk about the war in Ukraine. It is the first meeting of all three since February.
A war is a long fight between countries. Peace talks are meetings where each side tries to agree on how to stop. At earlier talks this year, the two sides only agreed to swap 314 prisoners. They did not agree on who should control a region called Donbas.
The fighting has not stopped. Ukraine's president said Russia sent 289 drones and 17 missiles in one night. More than 50 people were trapped under rubble after one strike. A short pause in the fighting ended at the weekend. People hope the talks will help, but it is hard.
levels.why: If the talks work, fewer people could be hurt and prices of fuel might stop rising.

levels.headline: Russia and Ukraine will talk about stopping the war
levels.body:
Russia has been fighting Ukraine for a long time. Now both sides, with help from the United States, will meet in a city called Abu Dhabi. They will meet on 10 and 11 November. It is the first time all three have met since February. They will talk about how to be safer and how to calm things down.
But the fighting has not stopped. Ukraine said Russia sent 289 drones and 17 big missiles in one night. More than 50 people were stuck under rubble after a building was hit. It was a school that was used to give out help. A short pause in the fighting ended at the weekend.
At earlier meetings, both sides swapped 314 prisoners. They did not agree on everything.
levels.why: The talks could help keep people safe, if both sides agree.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia will talk again about stopping the war
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine have been at war for a long time. Now teams from both countries, helped by the United States, will meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. It is the first time all three have met since February. They plan to talk about safety and how to calm the fighting.
But the attacks have not stopped. Ukraine's president said Russia sent 289 drones and 17 big missiles in one night. He also said more than 50 people were trapped under rubble after a school used for giving out aid was hit. A short pause in the fighting ended at the weekend.
At earlier talks, the two sides swapped 314 prisoners, but did not agree about the Donbas region.
levels.why: The talks are one way the war could eventually end.

levels.headline: Countries will meet to talk about ending a war
levels.body:
There is a war between two countries, Russia and Ukraine. A third country, the United States, is helping them to talk. They will meet in a city called Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. Talking is how people try to stop fighting.
But the fighting is still happening. One night, Russia sent 289 flying machines called drones and 17 big missiles. Ukraine's leader said more than 50 people were stuck under rubble. A school had been turned into a place that gave out help, and it was hit.
At earlier meetings this year, they swapped 314 captured soldiers so they could go home. But they did not agree on who should own some land. People hope next week's talks will help.
levels.why: People hope that talking will lead to fewer people getting hurt.

levels.headline: Grown-ups plan to talk about ending a big fight
levels.body:
Think about two children who keep arguing in the playground. A teacher helps them sit down and talk. That is a bit like what is happening with two countries, Russia and Ukraine. Another country, the United States, is the helper.
They will sit down on 10 and 11 November in a city far away called Abu Dhabi. They want to talk about how to be safe and calm down.
But the fighting has not stopped, and many people have been hurt. Ukraine said that more than 50 people were stuck under rubble after a building was hit. Talking does not always work the first time. Earlier this year they agreed to send some captured people home, but they did not agree on everything. People hope next week will be better.
levels.why: Talking is the best way to try to stop a fight.

headline: Democrats projected to win control of Congress in the US midterm elections

terms.meaning: Elections held halfway through a US president's term to choose all House seats and about a third of the Senate.
A president's power to block a bill passed by Congress.

levels.headline: Democrats projected to win control of Congress in the US midterm elections
levels.body:
Democrats have been projected to win control of the US Congress in the 3 November midterm elections, according to CNBC and Euronews, although some counts were still changing. Euronews reported Democrats on 220 seats in the 435-seat House, with 218 needed. CNBC's Election Desk projected at least 250.
Democrats were projected to flip Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, and CNBC also named Maine. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by 65 votes with about 95% counted.
A CNBC voter poll found nearly three in four voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor. Democrats plan to push a bill to undo President Trump's tariffs and to vote again on ending the Iran war. Projections suggest they lack the numbers to override a presidential veto. Some Democrats have also called for limits on AI data centres.
levels.why: Control of Congress changes what President Trump can pass on tariffs, spending and war powers.

levels.headline: Democrats set to take Congress after midterms that turned on the Iran war
levels.body:
Democrats were projected to win control of the US Congress in the 3 November midterms, though counting continued. Euronews put them on 220 of the 435 House seats, with 218 needed for a majority, while CNBC projected at least 250.
In the Senate, Democrats were projected to flip seats in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, with CNBC also naming Maine. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 65 votes with about 95% counted.
Nearly three in four voters told a CNBC poll that the Iran war was a crucial or major factor. Democrats say they will bring a bill to reverse Trump's tariffs and will again vote on ending the war, but projections suggest they cannot override a presidential veto.
levels.why: It limits the president's room to act and could change US policy on tariffs and the Iran war.

levels.headline: Democrats projected to win the US Congress
levels.body:
The Democratic Party is projected to have won control of the US Congress in the midterm elections held on 3 November. Counting was still going on. Euronews said Democrats had 220 seats in the 435-seat House of Representatives, where 218 are needed for a majority. CNBC projected at least 250.
In the Senate, Democrats were projected to take seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, and CNBC also named Maine. The Mississippi race was extremely close.
About three in four voters told a CNBC poll that the Iran war was an important factor. Democrats want to pass a bill cancelling Trump's tariffs and to vote again on ending the war. Projections suggest they lack the votes to overrule a presidential veto.
levels.why: Divided power in Washington can slow or block the president's plans.

levels.headline: Democrats look set to win control of the US Congress
levels.body:
Democrats look to have won control of the US Congress in elections on 3 November. These midterm elections take place halfway through a president's term. Some votes were still being counted. Euronews said Democrats had 220 of 435 seats in the House, which is more than the 218 needed. CNBC said at least 250.
Democrats were also expected to win Senate seats from Republicans in several states, including Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. One Mississippi race was decided by only 65 votes so far.
About three in four voters said the Iran war mattered a lot to them. Democrats want to cancel President Trump's tariffs and vote on ending the war. But they probably cannot override his veto, which is his power to block a law.
levels.why: It changes how much power the president has to get his own way.

levels.headline: Democrats are expected to win control of the US Congress
levels.body:
Elections took place in America on 3 November. They are called midterms because they come halfway through the president's four-year term. The Democratic Party looks to have won control of Congress, which is where American laws are made. Votes were still being counted.
In the House of Representatives, a party needs 218 of 435 seats to be in charge. One news site said Democrats had 220. Another said at least 250. Democrats were also expected to take several seats in the Senate.
About three in four voters said the war with Iran was an important reason for how they voted. Democrats want to cancel President Trump's tariffs, which are taxes on goods from abroad. They also want to vote on ending the war. The president can still block laws with a veto.
levels.why: The president now has to deal with a Congress controlled by the other party.

levels.headline: The Democratic Party looks set to win control of Congress
levels.body:
America held important elections on 3 November. People voted for members of Congress, the group that makes laws. The election comes in the middle of the president's term, so it is called a midterm. The Democrats, who are the opposing party to President Trump, look to have won most seats. Votes were still being counted.
A party needs 218 seats in the House of Representatives to be in charge. One report said the Democrats had 220. Another said they had at least 250.
About three in four voters said the war with Iran mattered a lot to them. The Democrats want to stop the tariffs, which are taxes on things from other countries. The president can still use a veto to block a law, so it may not be easy.
levels.why: It means the president cannot do everything he wants without agreement.

levels.headline: The party that is against the president looks set to win in America
levels.body:
In America, people voted on 3 November to choose members of Congress. Congress is a group of people who help make the laws. The vote was halfway through the president's time in charge. This kind of vote is called a midterm.
The Democrats look like they won the most seats. They are the party opposed to the president, Donald Trump. Votes were still being counted, so numbers can change. In one place, the race was only 65 votes apart.
About three in four voters said that the war with Iran was a big reason for their choice. Democrats want to stop some taxes on goods from other countries and vote on ending the war. The president can stop a law with a veto, so he still has power.
levels.why: It matters because it changes who can make decisions in America.

levels.headline: The party against the president looks set to win Congress
levels.body:
In America, people voted on 3 November to choose members of Congress. Congress is the group that makes the country's laws. The vote came halfway through President Trump's term, so it is called a midterm. The Democrats, who oppose the president, look to have won control. Votes were still being counted.
In the House of Representatives, a party needs 218 of 435 seats. One news site said the Democrats had 220, and another said at least 250.
About three in four voters said the war with Iran mattered a lot. Democrats want to cancel Trump's tariffs, which are taxes on goods from abroad, and vote on ending the war. The president can block a law with a veto, so it may not be easy.
levels.why: It changes who has the power to make decisions in America.

levels.headline: People in America chose who will help make the laws
levels.body:
In America, the grown-ups voted for people to help make the laws. This was on 3 November. The president is in charge of the country, but a group called Congress makes the laws. They share the power, a bit like a teacher and a head teacher making rules together.
It looks like the Democratic team won most of the places. The president, Donald Trump, is from the other team, called the Republicans. The votes were still being counted.
Many voters said they were worried about a war with Iran. The Democrats want to vote on stopping it. They also want to stop some taxes on things bought from other countries. The president can still say no to a new law, and that is called a veto.
levels.why: It means the two sides have to work together, or nothing changes.

levels.headline: A big vote in America might change who is in charge of the rules
levels.body:
Imagine your class votes for who sits on the school council. The head teacher has been picking the rules, but now the council might be mostly made up of pupils who disagree with them. That is a bit like what happened in America.
On 3 November, grown-ups voted for people to join Congress, which helps make the country's laws. The team that disagrees with the president, called the Democrats, looks to have won. Votes were still being counted.
Many voters said a war with Iran worried them. The new team wants to vote on stopping it. The president can still say no to a new rule, which is called a veto, just like a head teacher can. So they will have to talk to each other.
levels.why: It means different teams must share power and talk to each other.
